name: Tarnish-Bluff
geological_features: Oxidized cliff faces showing distinct color banding
Ancient meteor crater repurposed as a natural basin
Dead riverbeds carved into the tarnished rock
description: Tarnish-Bluff is a world that wears its age like a patina, its rocky surfaces oxidized into bands of rust, verdigris, and tarnished silver that tell the story of an atmosphere that was once thicker and wetter. Great bluffs of banded stone rise above dry valleys where rivers once flowed, their cliff faces a geological record of the planet's slow decline. Craters of various ages dot the surface, the oldest filled with wind-blown sediment, the newest still sharp-edged and raw.

The thin atmosphere carries a mineral tang and supports a wan sky that shifts between pale orange at the horizon and deep indigo overhead. Dust devils spin across the dry riverbeds with a faint hissing sound, the only natural movement on an otherwise still world. At dawn, the oxidized bluffs catch the light and glow like heated metal, a brief moment of warmth and color before the pale daylight washes the landscape to muted earth tones.

A terraforming initiative attempted to restore Tarnish-Bluff's atmosphere two centuries ago, installing atmospheric processors across the equatorial region. The project failed when the planet's weak magnetic field proved unable to retain the generated gases against solar wind stripping, and the colony that depended on the terraforming has been in slow decline ever since. The remaining colonists, numbering fewer than three hundred, maintain a stubborn existence in pressurized habitats, unwilling to abandon the world they have come to consider home.

The microbial life that clings to existence in sheltered rock crevices is a remnant of the planet's wetter past and is declining as the last traces of surface moisture evaporate. Biologists consider these organisms a priority for preservation, as they represent a unique evolutionary lineage found nowhere else. The colony's survival depends on supply shipments that grow less frequent each year, and the question of evacuation versus continued support has become a political issue in the sector parliament.
